newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey plans to tighten supervision on banking.
newsitem.headline: Turkey plans to tighten supervision on banking.

text.p: Turkey plans to change its banking law to strengthen supervision of its troubled banking sector and help the system adapt to Western standards, according to a draft law.

The draft, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, tightens requirements for bank owners and managers, forces banks to strengthen capital structure and increases the powers of the treasury minister and cabinet to take action when problems arise.
Under the draft, banks will have to increase their minimum paid-in capital to 4.0 trillion lira from one trillion and any change in ownership structure will require the treasury's permission.
The draft has not yet been submitted to the cabinet and it may take months before it is passed by parliament.

The draft says people with tax or social security premium debts or those who had shares of at least 10 percent in previously liquidated banks will not be permitted to set up a new bank or become a bank shareholder.
It also set limits on bank lendings. Banks will not be able to extend any loan of more than 25 percent of its capital base to a single borrower.
Lending to bank managers, board members, their relatives and employees are also to be restricted.
The draft forces banks to reduce their total equity holdings to 70 percent of their total equity by end-1997 and 60 percent by end-1999.
It also increases fines and punishment terms for banking law violations.

The treasury would be able to ask a bank to find new partners to strengthen its capital. Banks' ability to carry out transactions in money or capital markets might also be restricted under the draft, if needed.
The cabinet may decide on the transfer of bank assets to another bank or decide on the merger of several banks if measures taken by the treasury and minister fail to rescue a troubled bank.

International financial and rating institutions say the 69-bank Turkish bank system has been operating under pressure from chronic macro-economic problems -- high inflation, huge state borrowing to finance public deficits, unsustainable economic growth and an increasing trade gap.
They say Turkish banks, which finance a considerable part of government domestic debt at the cost of carrying short foreign exchange positions, face large foreign exchange and interest rate risks.
According to a treasury report, Turkey's 33 private commercial banks carried short foreign currency positions totalling $2.57 billion at the end of 1996.

"Continuous financing of Turkish lira funds by maintaining high levels of short currency positions may produce negative results in the currency market especially when economic and political uncertainities exist and foreign currency reserves are not sufficient," the report warned.
Three Turkish banks collapsed when the economy fell into a financial crisis following a run on the lira in early 1994.
Turkish commercial banks, including five state-owned ones, had total assets of around $83 billion at end-1996.
The state banks -- Ziraat, Halkbank, Emlakbank, Vakifbank and Etibank -- accounted for 38 percent of the total.

Economists say Turkey should speed up efforts to privatise state banks and cut domestic borrowing which hampers the financial system and crowds out private sector investments. ($ = 132390 Turkish Lire)
